sections.h2: Does Texas tax profit from selling a house?
sections.html:
Texas does not tax it. The Comptroller's office states that Texas has no state income tax, so a home sale adds nothing to a state return because there is no state return to file.

The federal government is the only income tax collector in a Texas home sale. Texas homeowners still deal with property taxes at closing, covered below, but those are charges for owning the house and not a tax on profit.

sections.h2: How big is the federal exclusion for a Texas home sale?
sections.html:
The IRS caps the tax-free gain at $250,000 for one filer and $500,000 for spouses filing together, as Topic 701 explains. The cap applies to profit only. Profit is what remains after subtracting adjusted basis from the amount realized, a definition Topic 409 gives.

Basis starts with the cost of the house, including sales tax and purchase expenses. Topic 703 says improvements that add value raise it, while items like insurance reimbursements for casualty losses reduce it. A Texas owner who finished a garage apartment or replaced a roof should dig out those receipts. A long-held house with no upgrades tends to carry a low basis and therefore a larger gain.

Losses get no relief. Topic 409 states that a loss on personal-use property, a home included, is not deductible.

Ownership and use. Each is measured over the five-year window that ends on the closing date, and Topic 701 summarizes them below.

Federal home-sale exclusion tests as summarized by the IRS
ItemIRS description
OwnershipTwo years of ownership inside the window
UseTwo years living there as a main residence inside the window
OverlapThe two years of ownership and use can come from different periods
Spouses filing jointlyOne spouse can satisfy ownership; each spouse must satisfy use
Back-to-back salesGenerally blocked if another home's gain was excluded within the prior two years
Extended official dutyWindow can be suspended up to a decade for service members, Foreign Service and intelligence personnel

Source: IRS Topic 701. Publication 523 lists partial-exclusion situations and exceptions.

sections.h2: How do I estimate my own gain before listing?
sections.html:
Work through the pieces in order and keep paper copies of each. The IRS describes the building blocks across Topics 409, 701 and 703.

  • Start with what you paid for the house, plus purchase-related costs such as sales tax that Topic 703 counts as part of basis.
  • Add the cost of improvements that added value, and subtract items that reduce basis, such as insurance reimbursements for casualty losses.
  • Take the amount you expect to realize from the sale and subtract adjusted basis to get the gain.
  • Compare that gain with the $250,000 or $500,000 ceiling if you pass both tests.
  • Only the part above the ceiling, if any, goes into the capital gain rate bands.

Sellers in Texas often forget that a home bought decades ago with little paper trail can still have a documented basis through closing statements and permit records. County clerk deed records and your original settlement statement are a good place to start.

sections.h2: What federal rates hit gain above the exclusion?
sections.html:
A long-term gain on a Texas house is taxed at 0, 15 or 20 percent depending on taxable income, with the IRS printing its 2025 thresholds on Topic 409.

  • The 0 percent band ends at $48,350 of taxable income for single and separate filers, $96,700 for joint filers, and $64,750 for heads of household.
  • The 15 percent band runs above those levels to $533,400 single, $300,000 separate, $600,050 joint, and $566,700 head of household.
  • Income past the 15 percent ceiling is taxed at 20 percent on the excess.

Depreciation claimed while the house was a rental can be taxed at up to 25 percent as unrecaptured section 1250 gain, according to that same page. Short-term results are taxed like wages. Thresholds change by year, so look up the IRS figures that match the year your sale closes.

sections.h2: What changes if the house was inherited or rented out?
sections.html:
The simple exclusion story shifts in both cases. For an inherited house, the IRS routes basis questions to Publication 551, since basis is not simply what the heir paid. Topic 409 also flags special holding-period rules for property acquired from a decedent and refers readers to Publication 544.

For a house that spent years as a rental, depreciation reduces basis, and Publication 523 handles homes with rental or business use. Title questions for heirs are covered on this site's Texas affidavit of heirship and probate pages.

sections.h2: When does a Texas seller have to report the sale?
sections.html:
Whenever a Form 1099-S arrives, even if every dollar of gain is excludable, and whenever some gain cannot be excluded. The IRS directs filers to Form 8949 and Schedule D for the actual reporting.

A seller who carried the financing over later years may spread the gain using the installment method. Topic 701 says the home-sale exclusion stays available in that case. Large taxable gains can also trigger estimated payments, and Publication 505 covers that rule.

sections.h2: How does the one-year holding rule differ from the exclusion tests?
sections.html:
It is a separate clock. Under Topic 409, an asset kept for more than a year yields a long-term result, and one kept a year or less yields a short-term result taxed at ordinary rates. Counting begins the day after acquisition and includes the sale day.

Picture two sellers. One lived in a house for 18 months and then sold: the holding period is long-term, yet the two-year exclusion tests are unmet. Another owned for 25 months but rented the place out for most of that time: ownership is satisfied while use may not be. Mark both dates on a calendar well ahead of any contract.

Gifts and inherited property get special treatment, and Publication 544 covers them.

sections.h2: Which Texas charges still show up at closing?
sections.html:
Property tax. The Comptroller explains that local units, not the state, levy it, and that appraisal districts value each parcel annually as of January 1. Because that is the date the year's lien attaches, a buyer's title company will want it settled.

Request the tax certificate early and compare it to what the county tax assessor-collector shows. The Comptroller's payment page lists the penalty and interest schedule that applies to unpaid bills.

Closing also brings a federal filing detail worth knowing early. If you receive a Form 1099-S, the IRS has a record of the sale whether or not you owe anything. Matching your return to that form avoids notices later, and a tax preparer can check the entries against your settlement statement.

faqs.q: Is there a Texas capital gains tax on real estate?
faqs.a: No. The Comptroller states that Texas has no state income tax, so a home sale produces no state capital gains return. The federal rules in IRS Topic 701 and Topic 409 still apply.

faqs.q: How long must I live in a Texas home to avoid federal tax on the gain?
faqs.a: At least two years of both ownership and use inside the five years before closing. The months need not be consecutive, and the two periods may be different stretches.

faqs.q: What is the exclusion for a married couple selling a Texas house?
faqs.a: $500,000 of gain on a joint return. One spouse can meet the ownership test, but each spouse must meet the use test on their own, per IRS Topic 701.

faqs.q: Can I deduct a loss when I sell my Texas home for less than I paid?
faqs.a: No. IRS Topic 409 says losses from the sale of personal-use property, including your home, are not tax deductible.

faqs.q: Where do I report a Texas home sale?
faqs.a: On Form 8949 and Schedule D when reporting is required, which includes any sale that generated a Form 1099-S. Publication 523 has the worksheets. A tax professional can confirm what fits your facts.
